findings.root_cause: SSH read loop uses a fixed 4096-byte buffer per read; under heavy output (`cat` of a large file, log streaming, Claude Code streaming long answers) the per-RTT syscall count dominates and latency scales with chunk count, not bytes.
findings.impact: Every SSH session under load — typical Claude Code session emits many KB/sec while streaming. Per-byte CPU cost climbs linearly with RTT count (RTT × syscalls = wall time).
findings.fix_sketch: Increase read buffer to 32 KiB or 64 KiB (matches xterm.js write batch size and PTY kernel buffers) and/or wrap stdout with bufio.Reader at the conn level so crypto/ssh is drained in one syscall per goroutine pass.
findings.verification: bench: feed 5 MB through crypto/ssh pipe; measure reads/sec and bytes/Read.

findings.root_cause: decodeOutput allocates a fresh `src` slice per call and copies `decodeLeftover + data` into it even when the decoder is nil-path; the encodeInput path also rebuilds the encoder on every keystroke via `enc.NewEncoder().Bytes(data)`.
findings.evidence:
src := make([]byte, 0, len(s.decodeLeftover)+len(data))
src = append(src, s.decodeLeftover...)
src = append(src, data...)
...
func (s *SSHSession) encodeInput(data []byte) []byte {
    ...
    out, err := enc.NewEncoder().Bytes(data)
findings.impact: Per-keystroke allocation in encodeInput; per-RTT allocation in decodeOutput. On a fast typist this is ~5 KB/sec of garbage that survives to the next GC cycle.
findings.fix_sketch: Cache a single `transform.Transformer` per session (set during SetEncoding); reuse its scratch buffer with `Transform(dst, src, atEOF)`. Persist the encoder side too via `s.encoder` field.
findings.verification: bench BenchmarkSSHSessionEncodeInput with go test -benchmem -bench=. ./backend/session/...

findings.root_cause: Write() copies the entire encoded input via `append([]byte(nil), enc...)` and stores it in lastSent; on a chatty session this duplicates every byte sent to the server into an ever-growing diagnostic buffer.
findings.evidence:
enc := s.encodeInput(data)
s.lastSent.Store(append([]byte(nil), enc...))
_, err := s.stdin.Write(enc)
findings.impact: Each byte typed is copied into lastSent (read diagnostic). Long Claude Code sessions accumulate the diagnostic buffer; memory grows unboundedly (only ever replaced, never trimmed) — contributes to the user's reported 400+ MB.
findings.fix_sketch: Cap lastSent to e.g. last 256 bytes via a ring buffer; do not store the full payload on every keystroke — store the tail only.
findings.verification: trace / heap profile during a long SSH session.

findings.root_cause: readLoop allocates two full copies of every received chunk: one for `data := append([]byte(nil), buf[:n]...)` and another inside `s.lastRecv.Store(append([]byte(nil), data...))`. Both copies are paid even when no diagnostic read happens.
findings.evidence:
n, err := s.stdout.Read(buf)
if n > 0 {
    s.RecordReadActivity()
    data := append([]byte(nil), buf[:n]...)
    s.lastRecv.Store(append([]byte(nil), data...))
    s.offerExpectOutput(data)
findings.impact: Every read (4096 bytes typical) → 2× extra allocations. Under heavy SSH output this is millions of small allocations per minute.
findings.fix_sketch: Pass buf[:n] directly to emitData (no copy); only copy into lastRecv on disconnect path. For offerExpectOutput, hand the same slice or a 0-copy view.
findings.verification: bench BenchmarkSSHReadLoop; pprof allocs profile.

findings.root_cause: LocalSession readLoop uses a 4 KiB raw `os.File.Read` on the PTY master fd, with no bufio wrapper, no deadline, and a non-blocking `select{ <-s.quit: default }` polling guard at every iteration.
findings.impact: Per-byte syscall cost dominates under fast output. The quit check before every Read also creates a busy poll pattern: even when no data is flowing, the goroutine wakes as soon as the kernel signals readiness.
findings.fix_sketch: Wrap pty in bufio.NewReaderSize(pty, 32*1024) for downstream reads, and rely on the quit signal only inside the Read via SetReadDeadline — no need for the per-iter select.
findings.verification: bench BenchmarkLocalSessionReadLoop under high throughput.

findings.root_cause: Every read allocates a new `data := append([]byte(nil), buf[:n]...)` then immediately calls `updateMouseTrackingState(data)` which runs `bytes.Contains(data, seq)` over up to 14 short sequences. The strip/inspect work runs on every single chunk, not on coalesced data.
findings.evidence:
data := append([]byte(nil), buf[:n]...)
s.emitData(data)
s.updateMouseTrackingState(data)
findings.impact: Per-RTT copy + 14× `bytes.Contains` scans on a tiny PTY chunk. On idle shells, the loop runs thousands of times per second when there is even minimal output.
findings.fix_sketch: Call bytes.Contains on the original buf[:n] (no copy) and only allocate when emitting to the onDataCallback. Coalesce consecutive small reads with bufio before invoking the mouse-tracking pass.
findings.verification: bench BenchmarkLocalSessionMouseTracking.

findings.root_cause: SerialSession readLoop uses 4 KiB Read and additionally copies each chunk via `data := make([]byte, n); copy(data, buf[:n])` before emitting, while also running `normalizeNewlines` which always allocates a fresh buffer.
findings.evidence:
n, err := s.port.Read(buf)
if n > 0 {
    data := make([]byte, n)
    copy(data, buf[:n])
    ...
    normalized := normalizeNewlines(data)
    s.emitData(normalized)
findings.impact: Serial ports are usually slow (< 115200 baud typical) so the read rate is bounded, but every read pays 2× small allocations.
findings.fix_sketch: Pass buf[:n] to normalizeNewlines (in place) and emit the same slice; only allocate the emit copy if the callback requires ownership.
findings.verification: trace / pprof during sustained serial output.

findings.root_cause: Telnet read loop reads 4 KiB at a time and immediately filters IAC inline; filterIAC allocates a fresh `var out []byte` and copies byte-by-byte. Under chatty telnet banners the IAC scanner runs O(n) per chunk.
findings.impact: Per-RTT copy + byte-by-byte IAC filter; on a noisy telnet banner this is a CPU hot spot.
findings.fix_sketch: Pre-size `out` to `len(data)` and walk with index appends instead of slice-by-slice (`out = append(out, data[i])`). For high-throughput telnet, batch reads into 32 KiB.
findings.verification: bench BenchmarkTelnetFilterIAC.

findings.root_cause: MoshSession.readLoop calls `s.moshClient.Recv(100 * time.Millisecond)` in a tight for-loop that wakes every 100 ms even when the session is idle (no UDP input).
findings.impact: Each idle mosh session contributes 10 goroutine wakeups per second. With 8+ tabs this is a dominant contributor to the user's reported 900+ wakeups/sec measurement. Each wakeup also re-acquires the mosh client state and pays an allocation.
findings.fix_sketch: Use a longer Recv timeout (e.g. 1 s) or, better, block on `s.quit` and a long Recv timeout. Add an event-driven wake path: mosh library signals when frames arrive, the readLoop blocks until then.
findings.verification: trace / pprof goroutine samples during idle mosh session; netstat udp recv queue depth.

findings.root_cause: Every Recv() result is copied via `append([]byte(nil), data...)` before emitData — even though mosh's Recv returns a fresh slice owned by the caller.
findings.impact: Each frame produces an extra allocation. Mosh frame rate is typically 1–10 fps when active, so the absolute cost is low, but redundant.
findings.fix_sketch: Pass the mosh-owned slice directly to emitData. If onDataCallback must retain, copy only when needed.
findings.verification: bench BenchmarkMoshReadLoop.

findings.root_cause: OutputLogger.flushLoop runs `time.NewTicker(logFlushInterval)` where `logFlushInterval = 1 * time.Second`. Every active log file creates a goroutine that wakes once per second for the entire session lifetime, even when no bytes have been written.
findings.impact: Every long-running SSH / local / Claude Code session that has logging on contributes 1 wakeup/sec. With 5–8 tabs open this is ~8 wakeups/sec just for logging flush loops, even when nothing is being written. Compounds the user's idle wakeup measurement.
findings.fix_sketch: Replace the ticker with a `chan time.Duration`-driven loop that wakes after `lastWrite + logFlushInterval`; or use `time.AfterFunc` that re-arms only when WriteOutput happens. Stop the goroutine when the underlying bufio.Writer is idle for N seconds.
findings.verification: pprof goroutine + runtime trace while 3 idle loggers are open.

findings.root_cause: OutputLogger.Enable walks up to 100 filename suffixes via `for suffix := 1; suffix <= 100; suffix++` and calls `os.OpenFile` with `os.O_CREATE|os.O_EXCL|os.O_WRONLY` per attempt, costing up to 100 stat+create syscalls on collision.
findings.impact: Cold start with 5+ open tabs paying 100 stat calls each is a measurable startup delay. Typical hit is on the first iteration, but the worst case is 100 syscalls.
findings.fix_sketch: Compute the suffix atomically with os.CreateTemp (or use a single os.MkdirTemp within the session dir); reserve a UUID suffix instead of a numeric loop.
findings.verification: benchmark Enable() on a directory with 50 prior .log files.

findings.root_cause: WriteOutput acquires `l.mu` and holds it across both ANSI stripping and the line-processor pass — which can call back into the lineProcessor's CSI parser. On a chatty session this serializes writes to the log while still allowing emitData to proceed (that's under a separate lock), but couples log writing latency to log formatting work.
findings.impact: Per-chunk lock hold time ~microseconds but compounds under high-throughput SSH. Strict scope: the stripper/lineProcessor don't need the file lock.
findings.fix_sketch: Split into an inner mutex guarding stripper/lines state and the outer file mutex around bw.Write/Flush. Drop the outer lock when the byte slice is empty.
findings.verification: pprof mutex profile.

findings.root_cause: ansiStripper.Strip allocates `make([]byte, 0, len(data))` for every chunk and the `s.pending = append(s.pending[:0], data[i:]...)` copy on incomplete tails reallocates the pending slice as it grows.
findings.evidence:
func (s *ansiStripper) Strip(in []byte) []byte {
    ...
    out := make([]byte, 0, len(data))
    ...
    s.pending = append(s.pending[:0], data[i:]...)
findings.impact: Every PTY read pays one stripper allocation and grows `s.pending` indefinitely for streams that produce ongoing incomplete tails (e.g. tail -f piping into a remote shell).
findings.fix_sketch: Use a pooled bytes.Buffer (sync.Pool) for `out`; cap `s.pending` length (e.g. 1 KiB) and treat longer incomplete sequences as malformed + drop.
findings.verification: bench BenchmarkAnsiStripper.

findings.root_cause: lineProcessor.Feed calls `out = append(out, p.line[p.emitted:]...)` and `out = append(out, '\n')` repeatedly within the loop on every byte, plus `out` is allocated per call (var out []byte grows).
findings.evidence:
case '\n':
    out = append(out, p.line[p.emitted:]...)
    out = append(out, '\n')
    p.line = p.line[:0]
findings.impact: Per-line flushes double-allocate: one for `p.line[p.emitted:]` and one for the trailing '\n'. On a `tail -f` of a busy log, this is a continuous low-grade allocation stream.
findings.fix_sketch: Pre-size `out` to `len(in) + len(p.line) + 8`. Use a bytes.Buffer pool. Track emitted via an index without re-slicing.
findings.verification: bench BenchmarkLineProcessor.

findings.root_cause: baseSession.emitData takes two RLock guards (outputLogMu then mu) and runs both callbacks inside the locked region of baseSession.mu. When the onData callback chains into Wails EventsEmit, every remote byte pays an extra lock round-trip and the lifetime of the callback extends the lock-hold window.
findings.impact: Per-chunk lock churn (2 acquire/release pairs per chunk) — fine in isolation, but in the typical Claude Code session with 50 chunks/sec per tab and 8 tabs this is 800 lock pairs/sec just to dispatch bytes.
findings.fix_sketch: Combine into a single RWMutex protecting both fields. Inline the load under a single RLock acquisition and store both callbacks atomically when set.
findings.verification: pprof mutex profile.

findings.root_cause: waitIdle busy-loops with `time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)` for up to the configured timeout. With 8 tabs each waiting idle at login, this is up to 8 × (5 s / 50 ms) = 800 wakeups per tab connect cycle. After connect, idle windows of 5+ s pay 100 wakeups.
findings.impact: Per-connect wakeup storm; contributes to the user's measured 900+ wakeups/sec when several tabs are logging in.
findings.fix_sketch: Subscribe to a per-session 'activity' channel that RecordReadActivity signals; use `select { case <-ch: case <-time.After(timeout): }` instead of polling. Increase idle granularity to 200–500 ms — 50 ms is overkill for idle detection.
findings.verification: pprof goroutine + runtime trace during a parallel 5-tab connect.

findings.root_cause: SessionManager.sessions map grows unbounded; Close deletes by ID, but failed/abandoned sessions (process crashed mid-Connect) are never reaped. The map also holds each session forever after Disconnect until the user explicitly closes the tab in UI.
findings.impact: Memory grows monotonically with session create/close cycles over the app lifetime. Long-running sessions (e.g. uniterm open for days) accumulate zombie Session interface values.
findings.fix_sketch: Add a reaper goroutine that purges sessions whose Status is Disconnected and whose last activity > N minutes. Or move Disconnected sessions into a separate 'graveyard' map that gets dropped on app close.
findings.verification: heap profile after 1000 create/disconnect cycles.

findings.root_cause: sessionStore keeps up to 2000 chunks of every session's data (MAX_CHUNKS=2000, TRIM_TO=1000). `getData` joins all of them on every read, producing a multi-MB string per session. With 8 open tabs each holding 2000 chunks × 4 KB = 8 MB per session = 64 MB resident in the Pinia reactive state — all of which is held in JS by WKWebView's GC.
findings.impact: Direct contributor to the user's reported 400+ MB resident memory. Each getData(id) call joins all 1000+ retained chunks — O(n) cost on every tab switch, every reconnect, every keepalive.
findings.fix_sketch: Replace the string array with a single ring-buffer string + offset cursor. Cap to ~256 KB per session (≈ 4× viewport). Add an explicit eviction on session remove that drops the SessionData entry from the reactive Map.
findings.verification: Chrome DevTools Memory snapshot before/after a 10-min Claude Code session with 8 tabs; expect per-tab retained size to plateau, not grow.

findings.root_cause: The legacy useTerminal composable creates a NEW xterm.Terminal and three new addons (FitAddon, SearchAddon, WebLinksAddon) per call without disposing the prior addons if the composable is invoked twice in the same panel (e.g. workspace drag-in reuse). The searchAddon in particular has no explicit Dispose() call in onUnmounted.
findings.evidence:
fitAddon = new FitAddon()
terminal.loadAddon(fitAddon)
let webLinksAddon = new WebLinksAddon(...)
terminal.loadAddon(webLinksAddon)
searchAddon = new SearchAddon()
terminal.loadAddon(searchAddon)
...
onUnmounted(() => {
    ...
    terminal?.dispose()
    ...
})
findings.impact: Each unmount leaks the three addons' internal event handlers + DOM registry. Drag-and-drop tab re-mounts (common in workspaces) compound the leak. Contributes to the user's measured 400+ MB.
findings.fix_sketch: Track all loaded addons in a list, dispose each in onUnmounted. Add a noopDispose stub for addons that don't expose dispose(). Modern components should route through services/terminalManager.ts (which already dispose()s the Terminal).
findings.verification: heap snapshot across 50 mount/unmount cycles.

findings.root_cause: resize() reaches into xterm internals (`(terminal as any)._core?._renderService?.dimensions`) every time it runs. On a typical session, resize is called by IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver, window resize, split-resize, and the retry timers in onMounted — easily 50+ times per second during drag.
findings.impact: Per-resize traversal of internal xterm state, plus the try/catch swallow makes hot-path debugging harder. cellWidth/cellHeight only change when fontSize/fontFamily changes, so re-reading them every call is wasted work.
findings.fix_sketch: Memoize cellWidth/cellHeight keyed by fontSize/fontFamily. Add a single coalesced debounced resize in the BaseTerminal (BaseTerminal.vue already does this — reuse its approach).
findings.verification: Profile Chrome perf during a window-drag resize; expect <1 ms per resize call.

findings.root_cause: getCurrentCommandFromTerminal scans every visible line (buffer.rows iterations) per Enter keystroke. Each line runs translateToString() (O(width)) + stripAnsi() regexes + PROMPT_RE match. A 80×24 terminal pays 24 regex matches + 24 stripAnsi regexes per Enter.
findings.impact: On Enter during a `git status` with 200 lines of output, we still scan 24 visible rows. The stripAnsi regexes are re-compiled each call (regex literals are cached in JS but the multi-regex chain still pays).
findings.fix_sketch: Track the last prompt line seen via xterm onCursorMove or scan the cursor row first (cheap), then walk up only until a prompt is found. Cache compiled regex objects at module scope (already module-level) — confirm no RegExp is created inside the function.
findings.verification: Chrome perf: record timeline during a `git status` + Enter to record suggestion.

findings.root_cause: handleInput uses `lineBuffer.value.slice(0, idx) + ... + lineBuffer.value.slice(idx)` (string concatenation) on every printable character to insert into the middle of the line. Each edit produces 2 new string objects + 1 new buffer string.
findings.impact: Mid-line edits (insertion in the middle, paste) pay O(n) per character. On a paste of 50 chars mid-line this is 50 × O(n) string copies.
findings.fix_sketch: Switch lineBuffer to a string[] + cursorIndex model (or use Uint8Array); expose concatenation only when read by downstream consumers. For mid-string insert, splice the array.
findings.verification: Chrome heap snapshot during a 200-char paste mid-line.

findings.root_cause: updateCursorPosition() walks xterm internals (`buffer.x`, `buffer.y`, `renderer.dimensions.css.cell.width`) every time a 0-ms setTimeout fires. updateToken is also called per character; per-keystroke cursor tracking has no throttle beyond the 0-ms defer.
findings.evidence:
const cursorX = buffer.x
const cursorY = buffer.y
const dims = renderer.dimensions
if (dims && dims.css && dims.css.cell) {
    const cellWidth = dims.css.cell.width || 9
    const cellHeight = dims.css.cell.height || 17
findings.impact: Each keystroke pays a 0-ms macrotask that schedules another defer. Under typing-burst the cursor position updates coalesce poorly.
findings.fix_sketch: Coalesce via requestAnimationFrame — only update cursor pos once per frame. The cursor suggestion popup positioning only needs to track the actual rendered cell, not be ultra-precise per char.
findings.verification: Chrome perf: typing benchmark.

findings.root_cause: terminalThemeGroups is a `computed()` that rebuilds via `TERMINAL_THEMES.filter(...)` on every dependency change. TERMINAL_THEMES is a constant module-level list, so the filter result never changes between filter invocations.
findings.impact: Theme select dropdown open on every settings change pays 2× full-list filter + array spread. Negligible CPU but unnecessary allocations.
findings.fix_sketch: Precompute dark/light partitions at module scope (const DARK_THEMES = TERMINAL_THEMES.filter(...)) and reference them in the computed.
findings.verification: Chrome memory: 100 opens of theme select.

findings.root_cause: BaseTerminal subscribes to the GLOBAL `session:data` event inside onMounted and accumulates state per session. On every KeepAlive re-mount the same listener is re-registered (generation guard mitigates but the listener closure is still retained). Vue KeepAlive cache can hold multiple BaseTerminal instances of the same panel, each with a full xterm + addon + scrollback buffer — visible memory bloat per inactive tab.
findings.impact: Each inactive tab in KeepAlive still holds the xterm canvas + scrollback (2500 lines default). With 10 inactive tabs, that is ~10 × (2500 lines × ~80 cols) of pixel buffer pinned in WebKit. Direct contributor to 400+ MB.
findings.fix_sketch: Drop scrollback to ~500 lines for inactive tabs (and restore on activation). Lazy-create the xterm only when first activated, dispose when cached for >N seconds.
findings.verification: Chrome memory snapshot: 10 tabs, 5 active vs all inactive.

findings.root_cause: releaseTerminal has a 500 ms disposeTimer that disposes the underlying xterm after all components release. During that 500 ms window, a fully detached xterm still holds its canvas + scrollback DOM nodes (moved to the hidden holding container in services/terminalManager.ts). If the user drags a tab back into the holding area, the terminals accumulate indefinitely until the session closes — adding up over a long day.
findings.impact: 500 ms holds during normal drag-and-drop are fine; but if drag-cancel patterns cause repeated acquire/release without steady state, terminals linger.
findings.fix_sketch: Drop scrollback when moving into holding (terminal.options.scrollback = 0 / release buffer) so the retained xterm is small. Or skip the holding container and use WeakRef-style lifetime tied to the Vue component instance.
findings.verification: pprof / DevTools memory after 30 drag cycles.

findings.root_cause: exportContent walks every line in the xterm buffer (`buffer.length` rows) and calls `line.translateToString()` on each, then joins them with '\n' into a single string and base64-encodes via TextEncoder + manual charCode loop. The `for (let i = 0; i < bytes.length; i++) { binary += String.fromCharCode(bytes[i]) }` is the slowest possible string-concat in JS.
findings.impact: Exporting a 5000-line scrollback blocks the main thread for ~50–200 ms (O(n) string concat + manual base64).
findings.fix_sketch: Replace the binary loop with `String.fromCharCode.apply(null, bytes.subarray(...))` or use the FileReader / `fetch('data:application/octet-stream;base64,' + base64Encoded)` indirect path. Process the loop in chunks of 8192 to avoid stack overflow.
findings.verification: Chrome perf: export 5000 lines, record script time.

findings.root_cause: sanitizeTerminalHistory runs 7 sequential regex passes over the entire scrollback string every time a KeepAlive tab restores. The pattern `/[^\u0000-\u007f一-鿿...]/g` allocates fresh match objects for every Unicode codepoint scan, and the function is invoked on every re-activation.
findings.evidence:
cleaned = cleaned.replace(/*{2,}(?:\u0018)?[ABC][0-9a-fA-F]{10,}/g, '')
cleaned = cleaned.replace(/\u0018+/g, '')
cleaned = cleaned.replace(/\u0008+/g, '')
cleaned = cleaned.replace(/[\u0000-\u0008\u000b\u000c\u000e-\u001a\u001c-\u001f\u007f]/g, '')
cleaned = cleaned.replace(/\uFFFD/g, '')
cleaned = cleaned.replace(
    /[^\u0000-\u007f一-鿿぀-ゟ゠-ヿ가-힯─-╿▀-▟←-⇿∀-⋿⟀-⟯⠀-⣿⬀-⯿]/g,
    ''
)
cleaned = cleaned.replace(/\n{3,}/g, '\n\n')
findings.impact: Restoring a 100 KB scrollback through 7 regex passes is ~10 ms main-thread blocking. With 10 tabs it can be ~100 ms on tab focus.
findings.fix_sketch: Combine the regex passes into a single scan via a single regex with alternation, or stream the input through a small state machine. Skip the pass entirely if scrollback is fresh from the active write path.
findings.verification: Chrome perf: tab-switch benchmark with full scrollback.

findings.root_cause: Each session:data chunk is run through stripCursorBlink (regex replace), then 2 .replace(/\u001b[2J/g, ...) regex passes, then stripAnsi (3 regexes via useTerminalInput.handleSessionData), then highlight (which itself runs 7+ regex patterns per line) on the FRONTEND for every chunk arriving from the backend.
findings.impact: Claude Code streaming produces 50+ chunks/sec; per-chunk this is ~15 regex passes on the main thread. Easily 1–3 ms of CPU per chunk, blocking UI input.
findings.fix_sketch: Batch incoming chunks in a 0-ms rAF coalescer, then run all regex passes on the coalesced payload once per frame. Use regex literals at module scope (already done — confirm no regex is in a hot closure).
findings.verification: Chrome perf recording during Claude Code streaming output.

findings.root_cause: exportContent calls `WriteFileBase64(filePath, toBase64(content))` which marshals the full scrollback to base64, then crosses the Wails bridge, then Go decodes and writes the file. For a 1 MB scrollback this is 1.33 MB of base64 + JSON marshalling + Wails IPC.
findings.impact: Single export blocks ~50–300 ms; not on the hot path but doubles the data on the wire (base64 expansion + bridge overhead).
findings.fix_sketch: Add a streaming WriteFile(path, []byte) Wails method; send the raw UTF-8 bytes directly. For very large scrollbacks, stream via ReadableStream.
findings.verification: Chrome perf: export 5000 lines vs 50000 lines; expect linear growth.

findings.root_cause: The terminal settings watcher does `deep: true` which means every fontSize/fontFamily/scrollback/theme change reruns the entire handler, including building a fresh theme object and calling applyXtermTheme. theme is a fresh object every call → xterm internal theme diff re-runs all colors.
findings.impact: Settings-panel edits (e.g. dragging fontSize slider) fire this watcher 60×/sec; each call rebuilds theme + reapplies. Visible stutter when adjusting settings.
findings.fix_sketch: Watch individual keys (fontSize, fontFamily, ...) instead of the whole object with `deep: true`. Debounce the resize() call.
findings.verification: Chrome perf: drag fontSize slider; record main-thread time.

findings.root_cause: resize() calls `terminal.refresh(0, terminal.rows - 1)` after every fit to force a full-viewport redraw. This is the "lineHeight / italic-clip" workaround mentioned in the spec: the existing render path may clip italic descenders, so a forced refresh is used to repaint.
findings.impact: Per-resize full redraw is expensive on canvas (forces re-rasterization of every visible glyph). With several resize events per second (drag, split, font load), main-thread cost adds up.
findings.fix_sketch: Set `xterm.option.lineHeight` to 1.15+ so glyphs have enough vertical room (no clipping); then drop the explicit `terminal.refresh(0, terminal.rows - 1)` call.
findings.verification: Visually verify italic characters in Claude Code output have descenders intact; measure resize() main-thread time.

findings.root_cause: xterm Terminal is created with `fontSize: 13`, `fontFamily: 'Consolas, "Courier New", monospace'`, scrollback 2500, but NO `lineHeight` configured. xterm defaults to 1.0 line height, which means italic glyphs (e.g. the ⏺ thinking block in Claude Code) clip at the top/bottom of their cell because descenders exceed cell height.
findings.evidence:
const terminal = new Terminal({
    fontSize: options.fontSize ?? 13,
    fontFamily: formatFontFamily(options.fontFamily ?? 'Consolas, "Courier New", monospace'),
    theme,
    cursorBlink,
    rightClickSelectsWord: false,
    scrollback: options.scrollback ?? 2500,
    allowProposedApi: true,
    allowTransparency: true,
})
findings.impact: Claude Code's italic thinking text appears cut off / visually broken. Compounded by the explicit `terminal.refresh(0, terminal.rows - 1)` in BaseTerminal.vue:498 — the refresh re-paints but cannot fix the underlying cell-height clipping.
findings.fix_sketch: Add `lineHeight: 1.15` (or expose as a setting). Consider also adding `letterSpacing: 0` for consistent width.
findings.verification: Open claude in uniterm, look at ⏺⏵ thinking block — descenders should not clip.

findings.root_cause: Unicode 11 widths are enabled via `terminal.unicode.activeVersion = '11'`, but there is no `wcwidth`/`charSizeCompat` override. East Asian ambiguous-width characters (e.g. ⏺⏵ used by Claude Code) still use Unicode 11's ambiguous=1 → may misalign with backend PTY (which often uses wcwidth -u13 or older). Also missing: 256-color code-block background (SGR 48;5;) — themes have only background, no codeBlockBackground.
findings.impact: Box-drawing and Claude Code spinner glyphs may wrap at the wrong column on mixed CJK sessions. Code blocks rendered by Claude Code look identical to surrounding prose (no visual distinction).
findings.fix_sketch: Set `terminal.options.charSizeCompat = true` (or expose a setting). Add codeBlockBackground to the theme schema; populate it for the built-in themes (subtly different from background, e.g. #0d1117 → #161b22 on github-dark).
findings.verification: Run a Claude Code session with markdown code blocks; verify the code-block bg is distinguishable.

findings.root_cause: xterm Terminal options do not enable italic font — there is no italic font configured. SGR 3 (italic) sequences forwarded by Claude Code's thinking-block markup render as upright text. The ItalicAddon (`@xterm/addon-italic`) is NOT loaded.
findings.evidence:
const terminal = new Terminal({
    fontSize: options.fontSize ?? 13,
    fontFamily: formatFontFamily(options.fontFamily ?? 'Consolas, "Courier New", monospace'),
    theme,
    cursorBlink,
    rightClickSelectsWord: false,
    scrollback: options.scrollback ?? 2500,
    allowProposedApi: true,
    allowTransparency: true,
})
findings.impact: Claude Code emits \e[3m for thinking blocks; without italic rendering, the visual distinction between prose and a thinking block is lost — blocks collapse into surrounding output.
findings.fix_sketch: Install `@xterm/addon-italic`; load it after FitAddon/SearchAddon/Unicode11Addon in services/terminalManager.ts. Update fontFamily to include a font that has italic face (e.g. `'JetBrains Mono', 'Cascadia Code', ...`).
findings.verification: Run claude, look at thinking block — text should render in italic.

findings.root_cause: xterm Terminal is not configured for DEC mode 2026 synchronized output. Claude Code emits \e[?2026h ... \e[?2026l to bracket a multi-line repaint (thinking-block redraws). Without SyncAddon / mode 2026 enabled, each line paints individually → flicker / partial renders during the spinner phase.
findings.evidence:
const terminal = new Terminal({ ... })
// (no SyncAddon, no enableSync option)
findings.impact: Visible flicker in Claude Code TUI as it streams thinking-block redraws across the canvas. xterm.js supports mode 2026 natively when constructed (it forwards the escape), but a SyncAddon instance is needed for the renderer to actually batch redraws until the matching l.
findings.fix_sketch: Install `@xterm/addon-sync`; load after other addons; the addon enables synchronized rendering for the bracketed pairs.
findings.verification: Run claude, observe spinner — no partial repaints during spinner phase.

findings.root_cause: WebLinksAddon is loaded but the listening addons (mouse reporting, bracketed paste mode) do not appear to be explicitly verified for compliance. Bracketed paste mode ("\e[?2004h") is mentioned as a passthrough in BaseTerminal.vue (bracketedPasteMode check), but no automated check confirms xterm forwards the escape.
findings.impact: If bracketed paste forwarding breaks (e.g. after a xterm version bump), pasting multi-line code into claude input is mangled into keystrokes.
findings.fix_sketch: Add a smoke test: emit '\e[?2004h' through terminal.write, assert terminal.modes.bracketedPasteMode === true. Verify mouse reporting modes 1000/1006/1015 likewise. (No production change — only a verification gap.)
findings.verification: Run unit test that emits the modes and inspects terminal.modes.

findings.root_cause: xterm Terminal is created without explicit `windowsMode`, `scrollback` is the only viewport setting. Alternate screen buffer mode 1049 is supported by xterm natively, but the BaseTerminal resize path does not preserve scrollback correctly across alt-screen enter/exit (the terminal preserves it, but Vue's terminal.position tracking does not account for the saved-buffer offset).
findings.evidence:
scrollback: options.scrollback ?? 2500,
// (no option comment about alt-screen; Vue side just calls terminal.resize)
findings.impact: When claude or vim exits alt-screen, scrollback vanishes (matches user-reported UX issue for full-screen apps).
findings.fix_sketch: Verify on the latest xterm.js that alt-screen buffer save/restore is honored — it should be by default. If scrollback is lost, set `terminal.options.windowsMode = false` (forces normal mode, not Windows-conpty alt-screen shim) and ensure BaseTerminal does not call terminal.reset() on alt-screen exit.
findings.verification: Run vim then exit; scrollback should still be visible.

findings.root_cause: writeClipboard first awaits ClipboardSetText (Wails round-trip); on false result, awaits navigator.clipboard.writeText (another round-trip). Each clipboard operation is a full IPC hop.
findings.impact: Copy selection pays 2 IPC round-trips on fallback; selection-copy is on the hot user path (every text selection).
findings.fix_sketch: Choose at init time which clipboard API to use (detect Wails availability once); use a single call thereafter.
findings.verification: Chrome perf: copy selection repeatedly.

findings.root_cause: installTerminalFocusRestore hooks a document-level mousedown listener that walks up the DOM tree on every click (`while (cur) { getComputedStyle(cur).getPropertyValue('--wails-draggable')... }`). Every mouse click anywhere in the app pays a synchronous reflow + computed-style read chain.
findings.impact: Synchronous computedStyle access on every click forces a style recalc and layout flush. On a UI with many nested panels (workspaces, splits) this is the dominant per-click cost.
findings.fix_sketch: Cache the --wails-draggable computed value per element on a WeakMap; invalidate on theme/setting change. Or check el.closest('[data-drag-region]') instead (a single attribute lookup).
findings.verification: Chrome perf: click 100 times in a workspace panel.

findings.root_cause: focusPanelTerminal retries with setTimeout(100ms) up to 10 times when xterm-helper-textarea is missing. With KeepAlive + drag, xterm's internal textarea can be absent for many frames — 10 retries × 100ms = up to 1 second of focus polling.
findings.impact: Per focus-recover polling at 10 Hz. Not on the hot idle path, but adds wakeups during tab-switch storms.
findings.fix_sketch: Listen to xterm's onFocus/onBlur events to know when the textarea is ready; or wait for the next MutationObserver tick on the panel DOM. Reduce retries to 3 with backoff.
findings.verification: Chrome perf: tab switch in workspace.

findings.root_cause: No App Nap / lifecycle handling found anywhere in the repo. There is no Info.plist customization (no NSAppSleepDisabled reference); the Wails macOS runtime defaults to allowing App Nap. terminal_io goroutines (keepalive, mosh Recv, output log flush) keep firing at full rate even when the user backgrounds the app.
findings.evidence:
grep -rn "NSAppSleepDisabled\|App Nap\|disablePower\|activityAssertion\|beginActivity" → 0 hits in repo
(macOS App Nap throttles background apps; Wails does not disable it by default)
findings.impact: Background terminal sessions continue waking at full rate — directly multiplies the user's 900+ wakeups/sec measurement whenever the app is in background. macOS may also keep the GPU/WebKit awake longer.
findings.fix_sketch: (a) Register Wails OnHide / OnShow handlers in app.go that pause keepalive goroutines and mosh Recv when the window is hidden. (b) For macOS-specific, generate an Info.plist entry that opts out of App Nap only when a session requires foreground network — or accept App Nap and ensure throttled goroutines are fine. (c) Add import _ "net/http/pprof" so wakeup sources can be profiled.
findings.verification: Run app, background, sample pprof goroutine — count of flushLoop/startKeepAlive should drop when hidden.

findings.root_cause: startKeepAlive ticker fires every 60s (sshKeepAliveInterval = 60 * time.Second) for the lifetime of every SSH session. With 8 tabs this is ~8 wakeups/min — modest, but still an idle cost that does NOT pause on app background.
findings.impact: Each SSH session pays ~1 wakeup/min on the idle timer. Compounded across all open SSH tabs.
findings.fix_sketch: When window is hidden (via OnHide hook), double the interval or pause until re-shown. On app quit, skip the keepalive entirely (Disconnect fires).
findings.verification: pprof + netstat for keepalive@openssh.com packet rate.

findings.root_cause: TerminalHistoryStore.Save writes the entire JSON file via os.WriteFile on every Save call (every command entered triggers Save via the UI). No write-coalescing or debounce; each Save produces a full file rewrite. Plain os.WriteFile is also non-atomic.
findings.impact: Every command a user types triggers a full JSON serialize + write of up to maxHistorySize (500) entries. Hundreds of full-file rewrites per active day. Crash mid-write can corrupt the file (contradicting STORE-09 quarantine).
findings.fix_sketch: Coalesce writes via a debounce timer (e.g. 500ms) and flush on shutdown; switch to atomicWriteFile for parity with ConnectionStore/SettingsStore; consider an append-only JSONL file.
findings.verification: tail -f modification time of terminal-history.json while typing in a terminal tab.

findings.root_cause: RecentStore.Record does not debounce — every Record call re-marshals the full id slice (up to maxRecent=20) and rewrites recent.json via plain os.WriteFile. Not using atomicWriteFile so a crash mid-write can lose the file.
findings.impact: Per connection-open and per reconnect a fresh JSON marshal + non-atomic file write happens. Inconsistent with the rest of the store package which fixed STORE-09.
findings.fix_sketch: Use atomicWriteFile; coalesce writes via a debounced background flusher; consider an append-only log.
findings.verification: Open + close connections in quick succession; stat recent.json mtime after each.

findings.root_cause: AISessionStore.Save / Load marshals / unmarshals the entire ai-sessions.json into memory on every save. AIMessageEntry retains Content verbatim plus an optional _rawApiMsg blob. No sliding-window or token-budget truncation.
findings.impact: Long AI sessions with large tool results blow up the file and the Go-side decode cost grows linearly. The frontend also re-clones this blob across the Wails bridge. Together this contributes to the 400+ MB WebKit memory pressure on long sessions.
findings.fix_sketch: Cap Messages per session (sliding window of last N turns or token-budgeted). Drop RawAPIMsg after it's been transcoded into the visible message. Stream-write the JSON via json.Encoder instead of json.MarshalIndent.
findings.verification: Run a long Claude Code session; monitor ai-sessions.json size and RSS via pprof heap.

findings.root_cause: SaveConnections emits the FULL ConnectionStoreData (every connection + group + recent) over the bridge on every save; the same full payload is then re-loaded by reloadStoresAfterSync on the next sync tick.
findings.impact: Connection lists grow unboundedly; emit payloads measured in 100s of KB for moderate users, MB-scale for power users. WebKit has to structured-clone the entire blob into JS land on every keystroke that triggers SaveConnections. Compounds with the 400 MB WebKit memory baseline — each emit can be retained until GC.
findings.fix_sketch: Emit only the diff or change kind: `{ kind: 'upsert' | 'remove', id, connection? }`. On sync reload, keep the full blob (it really did change) but compress with `sync/atomic` or only emit when the frontend's view isn't current. Add `omitempty` on zero-value struct fields so unused protocol blobs don't ship.
findings.verification: Chrome DevTools → Performance recording during a SaveConnections burst; look for 'structured clone' marker duration and heap delta. Compare payload size in DevTools Network (Wails frame size) before/after.

findings.root_cause: ConnectionStore.Save marshals the full ConnectionConfig slice (including PostLoginExpectSteps, K8sConfigInline YAML strings) with json.MarshalIndent even for a single-field edit.
findings.impact: Each connection edit re-serializes the entire list (KeyPath / PostLoginScript / K8sConfigInline can be large). On a 100-connection user every UI edit triggers a multi-KB JSON encode + atomic rename + fsync.
findings.fix_sketch: Use json.NewEncoder without indent (drop MarshalIndent in production). Consider a flat-file-per-connection layout, or at minimum diff-and-write only the changed connection.
findings.verification: go test -bench=BenchmarkConnectionStoreSave ./backend/store/...; pprof cpu for SaveConnections under repeated single-row edits.

findings.root_cause: CommandsStore.List does a full directory scan + reads every commands/*.md file via readCapped on every call. No in-memory cache; on each call it also reads commands.json and frequently rewrites it (the default-fill loop sets changed = true the first time a missing-pref is encountered).
findings.impact: Each call does O(N) directory reads + O(N) file reads + full prefs.json read + (often) full prefs.json write. On a commands-rich workspace this is hundreds of syscalls and full file rewrites per UI open.
findings.fix_sketch: Cache the merged List result and invalidate only on fsnotify events (or on savePaths). Skip the pref-default-fill write during read; defer the migration to a one-time startup pass.
findings.verification: strace -e trace=openat,read,write,fsync uniterm; observe repeated read+write on UI open.

findings.root_cause: SkillsStore.List reads every skill's SKILL.md (and probes references/ + scripts/ via dirHasFiles and countFiles, each of which opens a directory) on every invocation. No caching.
findings.impact: Every skills panel render or agent prompt injection triggers O(skills) file opens + a full prefs.json read + frequently a full prefs.json rewrite. With 50 skills that's 150 syscalls per List call.
findings.fix_sketch: Cache the merged list keyed by skills-dir mtime; use a single os.ReadDir per skill dir and partition files/subdirs in-memory instead of three separate dir reads.
findings.verification: strace -c -e trace=openat uniterm; compare syscall count on skills panel open vs a cached variant.

findings.root_cause: SettingsStore.Save marshals the entire AppSettings with json.MarshalIndent and atomic-writes, including CustomTerminalThemes (full TerminalThemeColors for each) and the Keyboard map. MarshalIndent allocates a buffer the size of the output for whitespace alone.
findings.impact: Every settings UI tick (theme select, font size bump, custom theme add) rewrites the whole settings.json. On modest SSDs the fsync blocks the UI thread for a few ms each time.
findings.fix_sketch: Persist only the changed subtree (split into multiple files: theme.json, terminal.json, ai.json, keybindings.json) OR write a JSON patch. Coalesce successive saves (debounce 250ms). Drop MarshalIndent in production.
findings.verification: Drag the font-size slider back and forth; observe settings.json rewrite count vs UI event count.

findings.root_cause: SettingsStore.Load takes the write lock for the entire duration of disk I/O + keychain backfill + default-fill. Any concurrent Save blocks behind it; the read returns only after the file is fully decoded.
findings.impact: First load on a cold start blocks all other Save calls (and keychain I/O). On macOS the keychain call is synchronous via the Security framework — a slow keychain response stalls UI load.
findings.fix_sketch: Use sync.RWMutex for reads, hold the write lock only during the keychain backfill + needsSave rewrite. Cache the parsed AppSettings in memory so subsequent Loads return instantly.
findings.verification: pprof block profile on cold start; observe the settings lock hold time.

findings.root_cause: ConnectionStore.populatePasswords re-iterates every connection, calls the keychain once per password, and if any plaintext passwords existed, takes the write lock and does an atomic write of the full file under that lock.
findings.impact: Every Load() on a connection list with N passwords makes N blocking keychain calls (synchronous Security framework on macOS). With 50 passwords that's 50 syscalls before the UI can render. Worst case: many tabs edit connections, migration rewrites the full file under a write lock that other tabs are waiting on.
findings.fix_sketch: Backfill passwords asynchronously after returning Load() (mark conns as PasswordPending so the UI can prompt). Coalesce the migration rewrite to a single startup-only pass.
findings.verification: pprof CPU + block on cold start with 100 connections; observe keychain stalls.

findings.root_cause: CommandsStore.CreateCommand / SaveCommand call os.WriteFile on the .md file directly (no atomic rename, no fsync) while also rewriting commands.json. A crash between the two writes leaves the .md updated but commands.json stale (or vice versa).
findings.impact: Two non-atomic writes per Create / Save / Delete, with a window where user-visible state is inconsistent. On power loss the .md can exist without a pref entry, or a pref can reference a deleted file.
findings.fix_sketch: Use atomicWriteFile (the helper the rest of the package uses) for both writes. Order: write prefs first, then the .md, so an orphan pref (no .md) is recoverable on next List.
findings.verification: kill -9 the process between the two writes; observe inconsistency.

findings.root_cause: copyDir uses filepath.Walk that calls os.Lstat + os.Open + os.Create per file with no batching. copyFileWithoutSymlinks opens a fresh file handle for each file and uses io.Copy with default 32KB buffer; for many small reference files this is overhead-bound.
findings.impact: Skill imports with many small reference files pay per-file syscall overhead. io.Copy uses a default 32KB buffer that is wasteful for tiny files. No bufio.Reader or sync.Pool reuse.
findings.fix_sketch: Use io.CopyBuffer with a pooled []byte (sync.Pool) and reuse open handles when iterating. Skip files with identical content (mtime/size check).
findings.verification: go test -bench=BenchmarkCopyDir ./backend/store/...; measure for a 50-file skill.

findings.root_cause: queryStrings and queryAny allocate a fresh map[string]any per row plus a fresh []any value holder per row. For a 10k-row x 20-col result that's 10k maps + 200k interface{} slots.
findings.impact: Big DB scans (10k-row table dumps) blow up Go heap and bridge-clone cost when the result is sent to the frontend. Combined with no streaming of QueryResult over the bridge the Wails call blocks for tens of MB of JSON encode.
findings.fix_sketch: Stream results back to the frontend via a Wails event or via paged callbacks. Provide a row-count cap. Use []map[string]any only for small results; for large results return rows + columns separately and stream.
findings.verification: Open a table with 10k rows in the data viewer; observe pprof heap inuse and p99 latency.

findings.root_cause: scanToString calls fmt.Sprintf("%v", v) for any non-[]byte value. fmt.Sprintf allocates a fmt.buffer + parses the format string per call.
findings.impact: Every non-string column (int, float, time.Time, nil) in every row hits fmt.Sprintf. For a 10k-row scan that's 200k Sprintf calls.
findings.fix_sketch: Switch on common types (string, int64, float64, time.Time, bool) and use type assertions / strconv.Format* directly. Fall back to fmt only as a last resort.
findings.verification: go test -bench=BenchmarkScanToString ./backend/database/... -benchmem.

findings.root_cause: Postgres GetTableSchema issues three serial round-trips (columns, primary keys, indexes) per call. For a database-tree UI panel that walks every table this is 3*N queries. MySQL/SQLServer have the same shape.
findings.impact: Open a 200-table database in the schema browser - 600 round-trips to the server. On a remote DB with 50ms RTT that's 30s of UI load.
findings.fix_sketch: Cache the schema for the lifetime of the connection; serve subsequent GetTableSchema calls from cache; invalidate only on user-driven schema mutation. Same cache applies to all providers.
findings.verification: Time the schema browser open for a 200-table DB over a 50ms RTT link.

findings.root_cause: mysqlProvider DSN sets timeout=10s but no ConnMaxLifetime / ConnMaxIdleTime / MaxOpenConns / MaxIdleConns. database/sql defaults to unlimited open conns and unbounded lifetime - a long-lived tab can accumulate idle TCP sockets to the DB, and a server-side timeout (wait_timeout) eventually drops them.
findings.impact: Stale connections cause 'invalid connection' or 'bad connection' errors after MySQL's wait_timeout (default 28800s) elapses. No pooling cap means a busy DB tab can open hundreds of idle sockets over a long session.
findings.fix_sketch: In NewDB after sql.Open call db.SetMaxOpenConns(10), db.SetMaxIdleConns(5), db.SetConnMaxLifetime(5*time.Minute), db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(2*time.Minute). Same for postgresProvider / oracleProvider / sqlserverProvider.
findings.verification: Inspect netstat for the uniterm process during a long-running DB session; observe open socket count growth.

findings.root_cause: No pprof endpoint is exposed; the audit's §8.2 prerequisite and the checklist's G item both flag this.
findings.impact: Cannot run go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile to capture CPU/heap/block profiles during a Claude Code session or any reproduction. The audit therefore cannot validate any wakeup/memory hypothesis, and end-users cannot diagnose regressions without rebuilding from source.
findings.fix_sketch: In startup() start `go func() { _ = http.ListenAndServe("localhost:6060", nil) }()` with `import _ "net/http/pprof"`. Gate on dev builds (e.g. const dev = Version == "dev") so production builds don't open a listener.
findings.verification: go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 with the audit's recording template; verify the symbol list contains wails_bridge.* and session.OutputLogger.* paths.

findings.root_cause: SyncNow / SyncTestConnection / SyncVerifyPassword / SyncConfigureRepo / SyncChangePassword / SyncDeleteRepo block the Wails handler thread on synchronous git + network + crypto work.
findings.impact: Every SaveConnections / SaveSettings triggers a.triggerAutoSync() (line 350, 488, 786). A user editing a connection field while online stalls the entire UI for the duration of git push+pull + AES-GCM decryption. With auto-sync enabled this happens on EVERY store mutation.
findings.fix_sketch: Return immediately with a request-id and run the sync in a goroutine; emit 'sync:started' / 'sync:completed' / 'sync:failed' events. Frontend already listens on 'sync:completed' so no breaking change. Add coalescing: only one sync in flight at a time, drop new triggers while running.
findings.verification: Add log.Writef timestamp markers; measure Wails handler round-trip latency in DevTools Network before/after — SyncNow should return <5ms instead of the sync duration.

findings.root_cause: SetOnDataCallback allocates a fresh map[string]interface{} per chunk and copies []byte to string (escapes to heap) for every terminal output byte chunk that crosses the bridge.
findings.impact: Per active terminal this is the single hottest allocation site. Claude Code's spinner phase emits many small chunks per second; each chunk triggers: 1 map alloc, 1 string copy (escaped heap), 2 interface boxings, and a Wails JSON marshal + WebKit structured-clone. For 4 concurrent terminals at 50 chunks/s this is millions of allocs/s. Directly contributes to the 400 MB resident set.
findings.fix_sketch: Replace EventsEmit with a session-scoped Go channel + dedicated goroutine that uses json.NewEncoder on a sync.Pool'd buffer. Carry the bytes as base64 in a fixed-size struct (no interface map). Better: have the frontend subscribe to a binary protocol over a per-session WebSocket and decode there. Minimum change: drop the map and pass `(sID, []byte)` to a wrapper that constructs the map once per emit and reuses a string-builder.
findings.verification: go test -bench=BenchmarkSessionEmit -benchmem ./backend/session/... — record allocs/op before and after. pprof heap inuse_objects on `runtime.EventsEmit` should drop to <1% of total.

findings.root_cause: moveResizeCh goroutine launched in startup() never receives a shutdown signal — it lives for the process lifetime, blocking on a channel that is never closed.
findings.impact: A leaked long-lived goroutine per app instance (always 1). Itself minor, but it's a sign the lifecycle model is ad-hoc: every other goroutine spawned in startup() is the same — `go a.autoStartTunnels()`, `go func() { syncSvc.Sync() }()`. When the user quits the app, none of these observe the ctx cancellation, so in-flight sync / tunnel bring-up can race with shutdown()'s os.RemoveAll(webviewDataPath) and produce 'sync failed' log lines.
findings.fix_sketch: Add `defer close(a.moveResizeCh)` (or signal via select { <-ctx.Done(): close(ch) }) in the goroutine body, and `close(a.moveResizeCh)` in shutdown(). For one-shot startup goroutines, branch on ctx.Done() before kicking off heavy work.
findings.verification: kill -QUIT the process during a slow sync; pprof goroutine count should drop to baseline within 1s.

findings.root_cause: triggerAutoSync spawns a fresh `go func()` on every store mutation with no coalescing or in-flight tracking, so a burst of saves (e.g. pasting 50 commands into QuickCommands) launches 50 concurrent syncs.
findings.impact: N concurrent git pulls against the same repo corrupt the worktree lock (`.git/index.lock` collisions), each leaves a sync:completed event the frontend has to handle, and the underlying sync.Sync() does not guard against concurrent invocation. Wakes up the goroutine scheduler ~10x more than needed during edits.
findings.fix_sketch: Add a single `syncInFlight sync.atomic.Bool` flag — if set, return immediately. When the sync completes, clear the flag and re-check whether another trigger came in during the run; if so, kick one more. Cap concurrent syncs at 1.
findings.verification: Burst-call SaveConnections 50x from a test; observe in log that syncService.Sync runs at most 2x (1 initial + 1 coalesced), not 50. Concurrent burst-test should pass.

findings.root_cause: chatCompletion* methods construct `&http.Client{Timeout: 0}` per call; no keep-alive, no connection pool — every LLM request opens a fresh TCP+TLS handshake.
findings.impact: Anthropic/OpenAI endpoints require TLS; reconnecting every turn adds ~100-300ms of TLS handshake + TCP slow-start on top of the actual model latency. Across a multi-turn Claude Code session this is several seconds of pure overhead. Wakes the scheduler 2-3 extra times per request (TCP/TLS goroutines).
findings.fix_sketch: Hoist a single `*http.Client` with `Transport: &http.Transport{TLSClientConfig: &tls.Config{...}, MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 4, IdleConnTimeout: 90 * time.Second}` to a sync.Once-built App-scoped field. Reset idle conns on shutdown. Streamed bodies do not need the client to be closed mid-flight.
findings.verification: Time three consecutive ChatCompletion calls with curl-equivalent payload. First call 100% handshake, subsequent should reuse (observe via `tcpdump -i lo0 -nn`).

findings.root_cause: Error-path response body reads use unbounded `io.ReadAll(res.Body)` with no size cap. A hostile or buggy upstream returning a multi-GB error body can OOM the Go process.
findings.impact: Any non-200 response from LLM upstream. Currently unlikely in practice but trivial to fix and the cost is unbounded.
findings.fix_sketch: Cap to 64KB: `body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, 64*1024))`.
findings.verification: pprof alloc on a synthetic upstream returning a 100MB 500 error body.

findings.root_cause: Every ai:done emit and the final return value both json.Marshal the full message map from scratch, with the same contentBlocks slice; double work per turn.
findings.impact: Per chat turn the full message (often 10-100KB for a Claude Code reply) is marshalled twice. With rapid tool-use turns the JSON-encode cost is non-trivial, and the same payload is structured-cloned twice in WebKit (once from emit, once from the return value).
findings.fix_sketch: Marshal once into a pooled buffer; reuse the resulting JSON for both the emit and the return. Better: skip the EventsEmit payload entirely for the final message and let the frontend pick up the return value through the promise resolution (which it already does).
findings.verification: Add bench `BenchmarkChatFinalMarshal` — confirm allocs/op drop ~50%.

findings.root_cause: SaveConnections / SaveSettings / SaveTunnels / SaveQuickCommands / SaveAIConfig all run a.fs-fsync on the Wails handler thread (atomic-rename write inside store.Save) before the emit; combined with F-203/207 this stalls the UI on every save.
findings.impact: Editor save → ~5-50 ms blocking (depends on fsync + connection-list size); combined with triggerAutoSync that can extend to seconds during auto-sync. Add up to per-keystroke for settings sliders bound to SaveSettings.
findings.fix_sketch: Run a.connectionStore.Save in a goroutine; return immediately with a request-id; emit 'store:saved' (or just 'store:connections:changed' if Save was best-effort with eventual consistency). For settings where the user expects persistence confirmation, keep Save sync but make SaveConnections async.
findings.verification: DevTools Performance recording while typing in a settings field; expect handler round-trip <2 ms instead of disk-fsync time.

findings.root_cause: panelLogTitle and EnableSessionOutputLog both scan the entire sessionToPanel map (keyed by sessionID) to find the one bound to a panelID — O(n) per enable on every Enable call.
findings.impact: Marginal: called on Enable/Disable only, not hot. Becomes O(n) when many sessions are bound to different panels (each reopen of a session rebinds). P2.
findings.fix_sketch: Maintain a parallel `panelToSession map[string]string` updated under the same mutex. Or invert to a session-keyed slice and update on bind/unbind.
findings.verification: Unit bench on n=10/100/1000 active sessions.

findings.root_cause: ListSessions returns every SessionInfo in the manager on each call; if the frontend polls this (it does — see panelStore and tabStore cross-checks) it produces a steady stream of allocations even when nothing has changed.
findings.impact: Each call allocates a fresh slice; on long-running sessions the garbage keeps accumulating. P2 because call frequency is moderate and the slice is small.
findings.fix_sketch: Either deprecate ListSessions and emit session:status events only on change, or memoize the last result and short-circuit when no underlying status changed.
findings.verification: Inspect store call sites; if a computed/listener wraps ListSessions in a watch, refactor to subscribe to session:status.

findings.root_cause: The `conversation` computed has no memoization; every reactive mutation on any message field (including per-token `content +=`) re-runs the entire 660-line transform: walks every message, JSON.stringify of _rawApiMsg, dangling tool_use filtering, pair validation, consecutive-user dedup.
findings.impact: Every Claude Code-style multi-turn session. Per token in a 100-message session: ~100 JSON.stringify calls on _rawApiMsg blocks + 4× O(n) passes. Hits main thread on every SSE chunk.
findings.fix_sketch: Compute conversation only when messages are added/removed (version counter), not when content mutates. Or store per-message token estimate alongside the message and update incrementally; cache the assembled Anthropic payload by messages-version.
findings.verification: pprof CPU on aiStore.conversation during a 50-turn Claude session; bench a session with `performance.mark` around computed eval.

findings.root_cause: `addMessage` wraps every message in `reactive({ ...msg })` and `_rawApiMsg` is a deep-tracked reactive value. Per-token mutation of `content` invalidates ALL dependents of every message proxy in the dep graph.
findings.impact: All AI sessions. Per-token Vue dep-graph invalidation. With 200 messages in a long session, deep proxies × reactive arrays (tool_calls, _rawApiMsg blocks) inflates the dep graph substantially.
findings.fix_sketch: Use `shallowReactive` for the message wrapper and `markRaw(msg._rawApiMsg)` (it's only mutated by the LLM, never bound UI-side). Buffer streamed text in a non-reactive string assembled at flush time.
findings.verification: Repro: open DevTools Performance recording during a 5K-token response; observe script-time per token.

findings.root_cause: `anthropic-beta: prompt-caching-2024-07-31` header is set, but the request body never has `cache_control: {type:"ephemeral"}` breakpoints on system / tools / last few messages. Static system prompt (~2KB) + tool definitions (~1KB) re-sent and re-billed every turn.
findings.impact: Every multi-turn Claude session. ~3KB wasted tokens + extra latency per turn. Across a 20-turn session that's 60KB of redundant input tokens, plus no cache-hit savings.
findings.fix_sketch: On chatCompletionAnthropic: insert cache_control breakpoint on `system` and on `tools` array. Optionally on the last 3-5 messages for incremental cache hits.
findings.verification: Inspect request body in Wails dev tools; compare cached vs uncached token counts in Anthropic dashboard.

findings.root_cause: `doSave()` is called synchronously on every `addMessage` / `addSkillCard` / `addCommandCard` / `clearMessages`, marshaling and crossing the Wails bridge with the entire conversation history (including JSON.stringify of every `_rawApiMsg`).
findings.evidence:
// aiStore.ts:419  await SaveAISessions(data as any)
// aiStore.ts:276, 296, 315, 327, 514  doSave() called from each mutator + after each chat turn
findings.impact: Every message add. Long sessions push multi-MB per save across the Wails bridge. CPU + bridge cost is paid per token (every tool result adds a message → triggers doSave).
findings.fix_sketch: Debounce doSave (e.g., 500ms trailing); only persist on explicit save / session switch / window blur. Snapshot delta (only the changed session), not the whole array.
findings.verification: Bridge trace of SaveAISessions calls during a 5-turn session; confirm ≤2 calls instead of dozens.

findings.root_cause: Every SSE `data:` line is fully `json.Unmarshal`-ed into a fresh `map[string]interface{}` allocation. Anthropic emits ~1 event per token for content_block_delta; a 2K-token response = 2K map allocations, ~99% of fields discarded immediately.
findings.impact: Per-token allocation pressure on the streaming hot path. Compounds with string-concat accumulator in F-307.
findings.fix_sketch: Define typed structs (MessageStart, ContentBlockDelta with embedded delta, etc.) and decode into them. Use `json.RawMessage` and field-switch on `type` for the small set of event shapes actually handled.
findings.verification: pprof allocs during a streamed 5K-token response.

findings.root_cause: Text delta accumulation uses `currentBlock["text"].(string) + text` (string concat) per token. O(n²) for long responses plus every concat allocates a new string.
findings.impact: Long Claude responses (multi-KB). Allocator pressure and GC churn during streaming.
findings.fix_sketch: Build a `bytes.Buffer` per block; flush to string at content_block_stop / message_stop.
findings.verification: pprof allocs during a 10K-token stream; compare n² vs n.

findings.root_cause: `chatCancel` is a single `context.CancelFunc` field with `chatCancelMu` protecting it. When two `ChatCompletion` calls overlap (retry storm, quick user re-trigger), call A's defer nils out `chatCancel` while call B is still in flight; `CancelChatStream` then becomes a no-op for B.
findings.impact: Stuck stream during retry storms or rapid user re-trigger; observed rarely but high-cost when it happens (request runs to natural completion despite user Stop).
findings.fix_sketch: Use atomic.Pointer[CancelFunc] and only nil the slot if it still points to your own cancel. Or refuse new chat while one is active (serialize at the front door).
findings.verification: Repro: trigger 2 ChatCompletion calls back-to-back; confirm CancelChatStream cancels both.

findings.root_cause: `estimateMessageTokens` does `JSON.stringify(msg._rawApiMsg)` on every message, every time the conversation computed re-evaluates (which is per-token per F-301). For a 100-message session this is 100 redundant JSON stringifies per token.
findings.evidence: // aiStore.ts:45  total += estimateTokens(JSON.stringify(msg._rawApiMsg))
findings.impact: Long sessions, per token. Pure CPU waste — the serialized form never changes for a given `_rawApiMsg`.
findings.fix_sketch: Cache `msg._tokenEstimate` at addMessage time (after JSON.stringify runs once). Track a running total on the conversation computed and decrement/increment on add/remove.
findings.verification: pprof CPU on `stringify` op during a 100-message session.

findings.root_cause: `activeAssistantMsg.content += data.text` is a deep-reactive mutation per SSE token that triggers the entire AISidebar render chain. With high-throughput models (Claude 100+ tok/s, GPT-4o), this is 100+ Vue re-renders per second on the main thread.
findings.impact: Every streaming AI response; visible jank during fast models on lower-end machines.
findings.fix_sketch: Buffer tokens into a non-reactive string; flush to `activeAssistantMsg.content` via `requestAnimationFrame` (16ms cadence). Use `shallowRef` for the displayed text so token appends don't churn the dep graph.
findings.verification: Repro: stream a 5K-token Claude response, observe Chrome Performance recording; aim for ≤60 renders/sec instead of N-tokens/sec.

findings.root_cause: Tool result blobs (execute_command output, capture_terminal screen, use_skill manifest) stored verbatim in `m.content`. A 200-line × 2KB capture_terminal = 400KB retained. The conversation computed (F-301) walks all retained blobs every turn.
findings.impact: Every multi-turn session with tool output > a few KB. Memory grows linearly with total tool-result bytes; per-turn compute grows too.
findings.fix_sketch: Cap tool result blobs at write time (e.g., head+tail truncation, or store large blobs to disk and reference by path/id in the message).
findings.verification: Memory snapshot after a 20-turn Claude Code session that cat'd large files.

findings.root_cause: `conversation` makes multiple linear passes over the message array: build kept (with token-budget break), strip leading tool messages, collect resolved tool_use IDs, second loop filtering, third loop for pair validation, fourth for consecutive-user dedup. O(4n + n·estimateMessageTokens) per chat call.
findings.impact: Per-turn latency before the request is even issued. For 200 messages this is multiple ms of pure JS.
findings.fix_sketch: Single forward pass that validates pairings, deduplicates, and emits output in one loop. Build the `resolvedIds` Set lazily from the same pass.
findings.verification: Bench with console.time around chat() call on a 200-message session.

findings.root_cause: `doSave` materializes a full snapshot via `sessions.value.map(...)` on every call (every message add). For a 200-message session with 4KB `_rawApiMsg` each, that's ~800KB allocated per save + bridged across to Go.
findings.impact: Per message add (couples with F-304). Heavy GC + bridge traffic.
findings.fix_sketch: Diff-based save (only the mutated session). Debounce to coalesce bursts. Pre-stringify `_rawApiMsg` once at `addMessage` so the JSON form is cached.
findings.verification: Bridge traces + heap snapshot during a 20-turn session.

findings.root_cause: Module-level `activeTokenUnsubscribe` / `activeAssistantMsg` shared across runAgent calls. Re-entrant paths (approveTool → runAgent; rejectTool/answerQuestion/dismissQuestion setTimeout→runAgent at lines 1056, 1082, 1099) call `registerTokenListener` which cancels the prior listener, but if an early-return path bypassed `cleanupStreamListeners`, the previous `activeAssistantMsg` may be replaced mid-stream without releasing reactive refs.
findings.impact: Rare re-entry paths; possible Vue reactive proxy leak (per F-302 amplifies this).
findings.fix_sketch: Make `activeTokenUnsubscribe` / `activeAssistantMsg` a single pair guarded by a version counter; ensure cleanupStreamListeners runs on every return path. Or fold re-entry into a single dispatcher.
findings.verification: Repro: approveTool while streaming; inspect Vue DevTools for orphaned reactive proxies.

findings.root_cause: `loadSessionsFromBackend` eagerly `JSON.parse`s `_rawApiMsg` for every message in every saved session at app startup. For 15 sessions × 200 messages, that's 3000 JSON parses; parsed object trees held in memory even for sessions that won't be opened in this session.
findings.evidence:
// aiStore.ts:147
_rawApiMsg: m._rawApiMsg ? JSON.parse(m._rawApiMsg) : undefined,
findings.impact: App startup with a large AI history. Holds multi-MB of parsed object trees in memory.
findings.fix_sketch: Keep `_rawApiMsg` as JSON string; only parse on session switch (when the messages become reactive and may be sent to the API). Or persist as JSON-encoded blob per session and parse on demand.
findings.verification: Memory snapshot before/after loadSessionsFromBackend on a history with 2000 messages.

findings.root_cause: `resolveActiveSession` spreads `panelStore.panels` Map into an Array and runs two `.find` passes (exact title + suffix match) for every command call. O(n) per call.
findings.impact: High panel count (>10). Linear scan per command.
findings.fix_sketch: Maintain a title→panelId index alongside the Map, updated on panelStore mutations. O(1) lookup.
findings.verification: Micro-bench with 50 panels.

findings.root_cause: Request body is `JSON.stringify`-ed once but uses a flat object with the full `AVAILABLE_TOOLS` array (constant ~6KB) and the system prompt + entire conversation embedded every call. There's no template caching of the static prefix (system+tools) — even though they are invariant across all turns of a session.
findings.impact: Couples with F-303 (no cache_control) — full tokens billed for the static prefix every turn. Per-turn latency: 1-2ms JSON.stringify on a 6KB tools array.
findings.fix_sketch: Cache the JSON-serialized `system+tools` prefix at session-start; concatenate with the dynamic `messages` only at send time. Add `cache_control` breakpoints (paired with F-303).
findings.verification: Inspect request body; Anthropic dashboard cached-vs-uncached token count.

findings.root_cause: Every SSE event triggers a `runtime.EventsEmit` carrying a freshly built `map[string]interface{}` payload (ai:block_start / ai:token / ai:input_json_delta / ai:content_block_stop / ai:done). These all cross the Wails bridge to the frontend, getting JSON-marshaled on the Go side and JS-cloned on the WebKit side. Per-token `ai:token` is the worst: a text-only delta plus the index crosses the bridge for every token of every response.
findings.impact: Per-token bridge crossing. With F-302/F-311 the frontend then triggers a deep-reactive mutation on the received data, amplifying the cost. Compounds in long responses.
findings.fix_sketch: Coalesce consecutive `ai:token` events in Go (e.g., 16ms flush window) before crossing the bridge. Or use a single WebSocket-like channel that flushes per animation frame. Drop unused fields from the event payload.
findings.verification: Bridge traffic count during a 5K-token stream; aim for ≤60 token-events/sec.

findings.root_cause: The k8s http.Transport is built without any keep-alive tuning: no MaxIdleConns, no MaxIdleConnsPerHost, no IdleConnTimeout, no TLSHandshakeTimeout — every REST call opens a fresh TCP + TLS handshake to the apiserver, even when called many times per second from the same tab (e.g. log streaming + pod polling).
findings.evidence: backend/k8s/client.go:50 base := &http.Transport{ TLSClientConfig: tlsCfg, Proxy: http.ProxyFromEnvironment } — no MaxIdleConns/MaxIdleConnsPerHost/IdleConnTimeout/TLSHandshakeTimeout. http.Client{Transport: &authRoundTripper{base: base, ...}, Timeout: 0}.
findings.impact: Every kube list/get/watch reconnect and every log stream request pays full TCP+TLS handshake (often 50–200ms each on remote apiservers). On a busy cluster running `kubectl get pods -A` polling + a log tail + 2 watches, this is 5–10 handshakes/sec just from k8s. TCP TIME_WAIT sockets also accumulate.
findings.fix_sketch: Set MaxIdleConns=100, MaxIdleConnsPerHost=10, IdleConnTimeout=90s, TLSHandshakeTimeout=10s, ResponseHeaderTimeout=30s on the Transport; reuse a single *http.Client per kubeconfig context.
findings.verification: Benchmark: kube REST calls/sec with -keepalive=false vs enabled. Check `ss -s` TIME_WAIT count on `wails dev` while a K8s tab is open.

findings.root_cause: On every watch reconnect attempt, runWatchLoop calls onEnd(err) — which under manager.StartWatch is wired to emit `k8s:watch-end:<id>` via EventsEmit AND reacquire m.mu to clean up the watches map. So a flapping apiserver triggers an EventsEmit + a mutex dance every 1s/2s/4s/8s/16s/30s.
findings.evidence: backend/k8s/watch.go:40-69 for-loop in runWatchLoop: `onEnd(err)` fires before `time.After(backoff)`. Manager wires onEnd to: emit event + `m.mu.Lock(); delete(m.watches, watchID); delete(c.watches, watchID); m.mu.Unlock()`. The next iteration immediately re-registers the watch in StartWatch and re-enters m.mu.Lock() again.
findings.impact: During a WiFi blip on a cluster with 4 watches, the frontend receives 4 reconnect-end events per backoff step (so 4 events at 1s, 4 at 2s, 4 at 4s …). Each emit also serializes the watch map lock against every concurrent StartWatch/StopWatch across all k8s tabs.
findings.fix_sketch: In runWatchLoop, surface onEnd ONCE on the first failure and emit silent `k8s:watch-reconnecting` instead; only emit a final onEnd when ctx is canceled or backoff succeeds. Defer the map cleanup to the success / cancel path.
findings.verification: Toggle WiFi with 3 watches active; EventsOn listener count for `k8s:watch-end:*` should drop from O(backoff_steps) to 1.

findings.root_cause: ParseBytes fully re-parses the kubeconfig YAML (yaml.Unmarshal + base64 decode + map allocations) on every Connect call, with no caching keyed on file mtime or content hash — and Connect is called every time a K8s tab is opened.
findings.evidence: backend/k8s/manager.go:88 ConnectWith → ParseBytes(kubeconfigYAML). backend/k8s/kubeconfig.go:98 ParseBytes does yaml.Unmarshal then three for-loops allocating per-context/per-cluster/per-user. No cache; tests construct fresh raw each time.
findings.impact: Opening 8 K8s tabs (different context switching) does 8 full YAML parses + 8 base64-decoded CA bundles + 8 TLS X509KeyPair parses. kubeconfig with 20 contexts ≈ tens of KB allocated and CPU'd per tab open.
findings.fix_sketch: Add a Manager-level LRU/single-entry cache keyed by sha256(kubeconfigYAML) → *Kubeconfig, OR key on file mtime when the YAML came from disk; cache also the parsed *tls.Config and the derived *http.Client.
findings.verification: Benchmark ParseBytes with a 20-context kubeconfig; verify GC pressure on tab-open vs cached path via pprof allocs.

findings.root_cause: Every successful REST response logs a 300-byte body preview via log.Writef, which calls fmt.Sprintf on every call and writes to a file-backed logger — paid on every k8s request, including polling calls fired many times per second by the frontend.
findings.evidence: backend/k8s/rest.go:55-59 preview := b; if len(preview) > 300 { preview = preview[:300] }; log.Writef("[k8s] %s %s%s -> %d bytes=%d body=%s", method, base, path, resp.StatusCode, len(b), string(preview)). string(preview) re-walks the slice; backend/log.Writef writes to a file each call.
findings.impact: Polling `kubectl get pods -A` (1Hz) + log tail calls + watch reconnects = dozens of writes per second. Each call allocates a formatted string and a 300-byte slice view, then performs a write syscall on the log file.
findings.fix_sketch: Move the body preview to log.LevelDebug gated by an env flag; for production builds log only status, method, path, byte count, latency.
findings.verification: Profile log.Writef under load: `go tool pprof -callgrind.out=cpu ./cpu.pb.gz`; check samples in fmt.Sprintf and *os.File.Write.

findings.root_cause: NewSyncService() runs synchronously inside app.startup and may invoke the OS keychain (PBKDF2 600k iterations + keychain IPC) — on macOS the Security framework call to read the encryption key can take 50–300ms, and PBKDF2 alone on the same keychain access pattern can take >500ms.
findings.evidence: app.go:186 syncSvc, err := sync.NewSyncService() — synchronous, in startup goroutine. sync/sync_service.go:35 NewSyncService → NewKeychain() → eventually GetEncryptionKey on the first Sync(). Note PBKDF2 is 600k iterations of SHA-256 in sync/keychain.go:107 (the cost is paid lazily on the first Sync, but startup sets up the wiring and keychain probe).
findings.impact: First-paint latency on cold start: any delay here pushes window paint. With macOS keychain potentially prompting for permission on first launch (depending on TCC), startup can hang visibly for several seconds.
findings.fix_sketch: Defer the entire sync.NewSyncService() body to a goroutine; expose a `sync.Ready()` channel that the SyncNow bound method waits on with a short timeout; in main.go/wails RunOptions set HideWindowOnClose=false so first paint is not blocked.
findings.verification: Time from `wails dev` launch to window paint with and without auto-sync enabled; check that it does not regress when the keychain is locked.

findings.root_cause: Auto-sync goroutine spawned in startup (and triggerAutoSync on every save) is fire-and-forget with no lifecycle hook: it will keep running Sync() (which does git fetch + push, PBKDF2 on each call, AES encrypt/decrypt) even when the app is hidden, screen-locked, or in App Nap — multiplying CPU/wakeups when the user can't see the result.
findings.evidence: app.go:200-212 if syncSvc.IsAutoSyncEnabled() { go func(){ syncSvc.Sync() ... }() }; app.go:619-638 triggerAutoSync fires on every SaveConnections/SaveSettings/SaveQuickCommands/SaveAIConfig. No IsBackground()/lifecycle guard.
findings.impact: Saving 10 quick commands in a row → 10 background git push+PBKDF2+AES cycles. With the app hidden the user pays the cost with no benefit, and on macOS each push wakes the network interface and breaks App Nap throttling.
findings.fix_sketch: Wrap triggerAutoSync in a debounce (200ms) and gate both the trigger and the worker on a `lifecycle.Active()` flag that listens for OnHide/OnShow; also pause when the window is minimized.
findings.verification: Run app hidden, save a setting 20 times rapidly; `ps -o %cpu` and Time-Wait socket counts should not spike.

findings.root_cause: Check() builds a fresh *http.Client with Timeout=10s but no transport reuse, no UA-cache, no If-Modified-Since / ETag handling — and the 5-min disk cache TTL only blocks identical calls within 5 minutes, after which every Check() opens a brand-new TCP+TLS to api.github.com.
